explanations.answer: This is the camp of God
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jacob sees the angels and says, “This is the camp of God.” (Genesis 32:2) Then he names the spot Mahanaim. The man sees angels on the road and his first move is to put up a sign for the place. I respect that.

explanations.answer: This is the gate of heaven
explanations.explanation: Good memory, friend, because Jacob did say something about the gate of heaven once, back at Bethel (Genesis 28:17). That was a different place and a different moment. Here on the road, he says, “This is the camp of God.” (Genesis 32:2) Then he names the place Mahanaim.

explanations.answer: This is the mountain of God
explanations.explanation: No mountain in this scene, friend. Jacob is on his way when the angels of God meet him. What he says is, “This is the camp of God.” (Genesis 32:2) Then he names the place Mahanaim.

Servant is the word, baker. Jacob tells his messengers to say, “Your servant Jacob says…” and to call Esau “my master.” (Genesis 32:4) I think Jacob is choosing his words very, very carefully. He's sending this message and he wants every word to be in its place.

Equal would be a bold way to open, friend. That's not what Jacob sends. He tells the messengers to call Esau “my master Esau” and to say, “Your servant Jacob says…” (Genesis 32:4) Nothing in that message sounds like two guys on level ground.

Protector isn't in the message, friend. Jacob has the messengers say, “Your servant Jacob says…” and he calls Esau “my master Esau.” (Genesis 32:4) The message is Jacob's, and it uses the word servant. He's not asking anybody to protect him in those words.
True, baker. Jacob says he's sending the message “so that I may find favor in your sight.” (Genesis 32:5) That's right in the text. He tells Esau about all he has and then asks for favor.

This one's true, friend. Jacob does say why he's sending the message: “so that I may find favor in your sight.” (Genesis 32:5) It's right there at the end of what he tells the messengers. A tricky one, because it sounds like something you'd have to double check.

Four hundred, baker. The messengers report that Esau is coming to meet Jacob, “he and four hundred men with him.” (Genesis 32:6) That's a lot of company for a family visit. I'd be checking my pantry for extra cookies, and I'd still be nervous.
Close, but the number is higher. The messengers say Esau is coming with “four hundred men with him.” (Genesis 32:6) Esau has a hundred more than that answer says. Jacob doesn't get to round down.

That's more than the text says, friend. The messengers tell Jacob that Esau is coming with “four hundred men with him.” (Genesis 32:6) Four hundred is plenty to make a person nervous. Nobody needs to add two hundred more.

Camps, baker. Jacob divides his people, the flocks, the herds and the camels into two camps. (Genesis 32:7) That's the first thing he does in his fear. I think a man who just heard "four hundred" wants to spread things out fast.

Armies sounds fitting, but that's not the word, friend. Jacob has his people along with flocks, herds and camels, and he divides all of it into two camps. (Genesis 32:7) The text says camps. Nobody here is lining up for battle.

Tribes isn't the word here, friend. The text says Jacob divides his people, flocks, herds and camels into two camps. (Genesis 32:7) He's splitting one group into two for a reason, and a tribe isn't that kind of split. Camps it is.
Escape, baker. Jacob thinks, “If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape.” (Genesis 32:8) Never put all your cookies in one box. Jacob is thinking the same way.

Surrender isn't in his plan, friend. Jacob thinks, “If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape.” (Genesis 32:8) The idea is that one camp gets away. Two camps give him a way out.

Fighting back isn't what Jacob has in mind. He thinks, “If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape.” (Genesis 32:8) The second camp is there to get away. That's the whole plan.
It's the other way around, friend. Jacob prays, “I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant.” (Genesis 32:10) He doesn't say he deserves it. He says he doesn't.

False is right, baker. Jacob tells God, “I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant.” (Genesis 32:10) He's not praying like a man with a list of reasons God owes him. I think that's a humble way to pray with four hundred men on the road.
That's his ask, baker. Jacob prays, “Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau.” (Genesis 32:11) He says it plainly and he says it to God. Sometimes that's the best prayer there is.

explanations.answer: Lead him safely back to Laban
explanations.explanation: Laban, the man Jacob had been staying with, isn't in this request. Jacob prays, “Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau.” (Genesis 32:11) He's heading away from Laban, not back to him. The prayer is about Esau.

explanations.answer: Send the angels to fight for him
explanations.explanation: The angels did meet Jacob back in verse 1, but he doesn't ask for them here. His request is, “Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau.” (Genesis 32:11) He asks God to deliver him. He doesn't give God instructions about how.
True, baker. Jacob says, “I am afraid that he may come and attack me and the mothers and children with me.” (Genesis 32:11) He's not hiding his fear from God. He says it out loud.

That one's true, friend. Jacob tells God, “I am afraid that he may come and attack me and the mothers and children with me.” (Genesis 32:11) He names the people he's afraid for, too. It's right there in his prayer.

explanations.answer: Offspring like the sand of the sea
explanations.explanation: That's the promise, baker. Jacob says, “But You have said, ‘I will surely make you prosper, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too numerous to count.’” (Genesis 32:12) He's repeating God's own words back to Him. Try counting sand, and you'll see why he picked that one.

explanations.answer: A land flowing with milk and honey
explanations.explanation: That line was spoken to Moses, Israel's leader, not to Jacob (Exodus 3:8). In his prayer, Jacob reminds God of this promise: “I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too numerous to count.” (Genesis 32:12) It's a different promise for a different man. Jacob is holding on to the one he was given.

explanations.answer: A throne that will last forever
explanations.explanation: That promise went to David, Israel's king, much later (2 Samuel 7:16). Jacob's prayer ends with a different one: “I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too numerous to count.” (Genesis 32:12) He's quoting what God said to him. Throne promises aren't in this prayer.

A gift, baker. Jacob spends the night there, and from what he had brought with him, he selects a gift for his brother Esau. (Genesis 32:13) He's picking it out himself. Nobody's handing him a gift card.
No loan here, friend. The text says Jacob selects “a gift for his brother Esau.” (Genesis 32:13) A loan comes back, but a gift is given. Jacob is giving.

Nobody's haggling in this verse. Jacob selects a gift from what he brought, and the text calls it “a gift for his brother Esau.” (Genesis 32:13) A trade would mean getting something back. A gift is just a gift.

That's his instruction, baker. Jacob entrusts the animals to his servants in separate herds and says, “Go on ahead of me, and keep some distance between the herds.” (Genesis 32:16) The herds are separate and they stay spread out. I think that's how you get Esau to meet them one at a time.
He says the opposite, friend. The herds go in separate groups, and Jacob tells the servants, “keep some distance between the herds.” (Genesis 32:16) Bunching up isn't the plan. Spread out is.

Nothing about night travel here, friend. Jacob tells his servants, “Go on ahead of me, and keep some distance between the herds.” (Genesis 32:16) His order is about distance. The time of day never comes up in that verse.

Right, baker. The servant is to say, “They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift, sent to my lord Esau.” (Genesis 32:18) Jacob wrote the lines, and he's the one named in them. He makes sure Esau hears the name from the very first herd.

Laban is Jacob's relative whose household Jacob had been staying in (Genesis 32:4). He's not in this answer. The servant is to say, “They belong to your servant Jacob.” (Genesis 32:18) The animals are Jacob's gift.

Isaac is Jacob's father (Genesis 32:9), but the herds aren't named for him here. The servant is to say, “They belong to your servant Jacob.” (Genesis 32:18) The gift comes from Jacob. Esau is supposed to know that right away.
True, baker. The servant is to say, “And behold, Jacob is behind us.” (Genesis 32:18) Esau hears about the gift and about Jacob in one breath. That's a lot to pack into a speech.

This one's true, friend. Jacob tells the lead servant to say, “And behold, Jacob is behind us.” (Genesis 32:18) It comes right after the part about the gift. The servant has two jobs: say the gift is from Jacob, and say Jacob is coming.

explanations.answer: Win Esau over before they meet
explanations.explanation: That's what he's hoping, baker. Jacob thinks, “I will appease Esau with the gift that is going before me. After that I can face him, and perhaps he will accept me.” (Genesis 32:20) The gift goes first and Jacob comes after. He's trying to soften Esau up before Esau sees his face.

explanations.answer: Pay Esau for crossing his land
explanations.explanation: No toll booth in this verse, friend. Jacob thinks, “I will appease Esau with the gift that is going before me.” (Genesis 32:20) The gift is to appease Esau. Land isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: Show Esau how rich Jacob is
explanations.explanation: Jacob's words are about something else, friend. He thinks, “I will appease Esau with the gift that is going before me. After that I can face him, and perhaps he will accept me.” (Genesis 32:20) That's what he's hoping for. The text doesn't say he's showing off.
Not quite, friend. Jacob thinks, “After that I can face him, and perhaps he will accept me.” (Genesis 32:20) Notice the word perhaps. A man who was sure wouldn't need a parade of herds.
False is right, baker. Jacob thinks, “perhaps he will accept me.” (Genesis 32:20) He's hoping, not sure. Perhaps is a small word, but it's doing a lot of work in that sentence.
